claims.source: However, the core ring system of 2a is tilted toward helix βH6 and strand βS7 by ~20° (angle between the two C1-C9 axes; rmsdbacIII-2a of 0.794 Å for 39 core atoms), thereby adopting a pose that is closer to that observed for paclitaxel bound to straight tubulin in microtubules (PDB ID 6WVR; rmsd2a-paclitaxel of 0.845 Å for 56 core atoms; rmsdbacIII-paclitaxel of 1.048 Å for 42 core atoms; Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison and RMSD calculations.

claims.claim: The C39 carbonyl of the C13-3'-N-acrylamide moiety of 2a forms a hydrogen bond to the βH229 NE2 in curved tubulin, similar to paclitaxel bound to straight tubulin.
claims.source: Similar to paclitaxel bound to straight tubulin, the C39 carbonyl of the C13-3'-N-acrylamide moiety of 2a forms a hydrogen bond to the βH229 NE2 in curved tubulin (Figures 3B and 4B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figures 3B and 4B.

claims.claim: The terminal ester moiety of 2a is exposed to the solvent and forms water-mediated hydrogen bonds to the side chains of βE22 and βR369 of β-tubulin.
claims.source: The terminal ester moiety of 2a is exposed to the solvent and it forms water-mediated hydrogen bonds to the side chains of βE22 and βR369 of β-tubulin; it lodges within a space that is otherwise occupied by crystallographic water molecules in the curved tubulin-baccatin III structure.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The favorable hydrogen bond network established by 2a cannot be established by the 3'-N-benzamido phenyl ring A of paclitaxel in the curved tubulin conformation.
claims.source: This favorable hydrogen bond network cannot be established by the 3'-N-benzamido phenyl ring A of paclitaxel in the curved tubulin conformation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison.

claims.claim: In the context of paclitaxel-bound microtubules, helix H1 moves closer toward helix H7, allowing side chains of Lys19, Glu22, and Val23 to form a hydrophobic cavity that stabilizes the A ring.
claims.source: In the context of paclitaxel-bound microtubules (straight tubulin), the helix H1 moves closer toward helix H7, thereby allowing these three side chains to form a hydrophobic cavity that stabilizes the A ring, which suggest a structural mechanism for the higher affinity of paclitaxel observed for the straight tubulin conformation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison between curved and straight tubulin conformations.

claims.claim: The helix H1 movement causes the side chain of βD26 to occupy the space of the βR369 side chain, which adopts a flipped-out conformation, providing additional stabilization through a polar interaction to the 3' amide nitrogen of paclitaxel.
claims.source: Moreover, the helix H1 movement causes the side chain of βD26 to occupy the space of the βR369 side chain, which adopts a flipped-out conformation. This arrangement provides additional stabilization through a polar interaction to the 3' amide nitrogen of paclitaxel and supports a more favorable binding of paclitaxel to microtubules (Figures 3B and 4B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figures 3B and 4B.

claims.claim: The absence of the C10 acetate in 2a relative to baccatin III has little impact on the conformation of the secondary structural elements that shape the taxane site.
claims.source: The absence of the C10 acetate in 2a relative to baccatin III has little impact on the conformation of the secondary structural elements that shape the taxane site (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The main interaction energy of taxanes is mediated by their common baccatin III core moieties.
claims.source: Together, these structural data provide – for the first time – a high-resolution structural description of the interaction of taxanes harboring a C13 side chain with unassembled, curved tubulin. They indicate that the main interaction energy of this class of antitubulin agents is mediated by their common baccatin III core moieties.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural data presented.

claims.claim: The taxane pose in both curved and straight tubulin is very similar.
claims.source: They further reveal that the taxane pose in both curved and straight tubulin is very similar; however, subtle structural details reveal why paclitaxel binds more favorably to straight tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: Significant conformational changes were observed for backbone atoms of the βT5 loop and the N-terminal segment of the βM loop in both the tubulin-baccatin III and tubulin-2a complex structures.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5, significant and comparable conformational changes were observed for backbone atoms of the βT5 loop and the N-terminal segment of the βM loop in both the tubulin-baccatin III and tubulin-2a complex structures.
claims.evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The βT5 loop is oriented in the active 'out' conformation in both tubulin-baccatin III and tubulin-2a structures.
claims.source: Interestingly, the βT5 loop that is prominently involved in establishing longitudinal tubulin contacts along protofilaments is oriented in the active 'out' conformation in both structures (Nawrotek et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures and supported by a literature citation.

claims.claim: There is an allosteric crosstalk between the taxane site and the βT5 loop possibly via the central helix βH7 and the guanosine nucleotide bound to β-tubulin.
claims.source: This observation indicates an allosteric crosstalk between the taxane site and the βT5 loop possibly via the central helix βH7 and the guanosine nucleotide bound to β-tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claims.claim: Well-defined electron densities for the βM loop were found only for its N-terminal section up to residue βR278, while the remaining portion of the loop appeared disordered in both baccatin III and 2a complex structures.
claims.source: In the case of the βM loop, we only found well-defined electron densities for its N-terminal section up to residue βR278, while the remaining portion of the loop appeared disordered in both complex structures.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claims.claim: Partial βM loop structuring has been observed previously in tubulin complexes with the taxane-site ligands dictyostatin and discodermolide.
claims.source: This partial βM loop structuring has been observed previously in tubulin complexes with the taxane-site ligands dictyostatin and discodermolide (Trigili et al., 2016; Prota et al., 2017; note that the taxane-site ligands zampanolide and epothilone A promote the structuring of the βM loop into a helical conformation Prota et al., 2013a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: A direct effect of taxanes on the βM loop is consistent with the notion that paclitaxel stabilizes this secondary structural element in two discrete conformations giving rise to heterogeneous lateral microtubule-lattice contacts.
claims.source: A direct effect of taxanes on the βM loop is consistent with the notion that paclitaxel stabilizes this secondary structural element in two discrete conformations giving rise to heterogeneous lateral microtubule-lattice contacts (Debs et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claims.claim: Significant conformational changes were found in the βS9-βS10 loop, which were more prominent in tubulin-2a than in tubulin-baccatin III.
claims.source: We also found significant conformational changes in the βS9-βS10 loop, which were more prominent in tubulin-2a than in tubulin-baccatin III.
claims.evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis.

claims.claim: The presence of a C13 side chain in 2a needs more room for accommodation inside the taxane site compared to baccatin III, which lacks a C13 side chain.
claims.source: This finding can be explained by the presence of a C13 side chain in 2a that needs more room for accommodation inside the taxane site compared to baccatin III, which lacks a C13 side chain.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claims.claim: A conformational change of the H2' helix was observed in the tubulin-baccatin III structure, which was absent in tubulin-2a.
claims.source: Finally, we observed a conformational change of the H2' helix in the tubulin-baccatin III structure, which was absent in tubulin-2a.
claims.evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis.

claims.claim: Binding of baccatin III to curved tubulin causes a subtle relative twist between the N-terminal and the intermediate domains of β-tubulin.
claims.source: For tubulin-baccatin III, a subtle relative twist between the N-terminal and the intermediate domains was observed (Figure 6; Videos 1 and 2), while binding of 2a rather caused both the N-terminal and intermediate domains of β-tubulin to move slightly apart (Figure 6; Videos 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 6 and Videos 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Binding of 2a to curved tubulin causes both the N-terminal and intermediate domains of β-tubulin to move slightly apart.
claims.source: For tubulin-baccatin III, a subtle relative twist between the N-terminal and the intermediate domains was observed (Figure 6; Videos 1 and 2), while binding of 2a rather caused both the N-terminal and intermediate domains of β-tubulin to move slightly apart (Figure 6; Videos 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 6 and Videos 3 and 4.

claims.claim: Taxane binding to tubulin causes global, but subtle conformational rearrangements.
claims.source: Thus, taxane binding to tubulin causes global, but subtle conformational rearrangements.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural analyses.

claims.claim: Similar significant conformational changes of both the βT5 and the βM loops were observed upon paclitaxel binding to straight tubulin in microtubules as observed for taxanes bound to curved tubulin.
claims.source: The rmsd analysis revealed similar significant conformational changes of both the βT5 and the βM loops as observed for the taxanes bound to curved tubulin, however, no prominent perturbations of the βS9-βS10 loop could be detected.
claims.evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis comparing paclitaxel-bound and apo microtubules.

claims.claim: No prominent perturbations of the βS9-βS10 loop were detected upon paclitaxel binding to straight tubulin in microtubules.
claims.source: The rmsd analysis revealed similar significant conformational changes of both the βT5 and the βM loops as observed for the taxanes bound to curved tubulin, however, no prominent perturbations of the βS9-βS10 loop could be detected.
claims.evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis.

claims.claim: Significant conformational changes of the 'βS2-βS2'' loop and the C-terminal βH11-βH12 helix region were found upon paclitaxel binding to microtubules, which were not detected in the curved tubulin structures.
claims.source: In addition, we found significant conformational changes of the 'βS2-βS2'' loop (the secondary structural elements that interact with the βM loop of the neighboring protofilament) and the C-terminal βH11-βH12 helix region (Figure 4C and D), which were not detected in the curved tubulin structures.
claims.evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: Taxane binding in the context of the microtubule has an effect on the lateral contact established by the βM loop.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that taxane binding in the context of the microtubule have an effect on the lateral contact established by the βM loop, an effect that cannot be detected in curved tubulin as this contact does not exist in the crystal.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claims.claim: The tubulin dimer rise increased by 0.24 nm (from 8.12±0.02 to 8.36±0.02 nm) in the presence of GMPCPP compared to GTP.
claims.source: We first analyzed microtubules that were assembled in the presence of either guanosine triphosphate (GTP) (producing GDP-microtubules) or the slowly hydrolyzable GTP analogue GMPCPP (producing GMPCPP-microtubules) and found that the tubulin dimer rise increased by 0.24 nm (from 8.12±0.02 to 8.36±0.02 nm, respectively) in the presence of GMPCPP, a distance that is consistent with that found in previous studies.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claims.claim: The microtubule radius increased from 11.42±0.1 nm for GDP-microtubules to 11.63±0.1 nm for GMPCPP-microtubules.
claims.source: Concomitantly, the microtubule radius increased from 11.42±0.1 nm for GDP-microtubules to 11.63±0.1 nm for GMPCPP-microtubules, which translates into an increase of the average protofilament number (av. PF nr.) from 12.9 to 13.3, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claims.claim: An increase in both tubulin dimer rise and number of protofilaments for GMPCPP-microtubules compared to GDP-microtubules has been reported previously.
claims.source: An increase in both tubulin dimer rise and number of protofilaments for GMPCPP-microtubules compared to GDP-microtubules has been reported previously (Vale et al., 1994; Alushin et al., 2014; Hyman et al., 1992; Yajima et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claims.claim: Both paclitaxel-bound microtubules and docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a similar lattice expansion of 0.24 nm as seen for GMPCPP-bound microtubules when compared to GDP-bound microtubules.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 7 and Table 2, and when compared to GDP-bound microtubules, both paclitaxel-bound microtubules and docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a similar lattice expansion of 0.24 nm as seen for GMPCPP-bound microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements shown in Figure 7 and Table 2.

claims.claim: Paclitaxel-bound microtubules show a reduced microtubule radius of 10.97±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.21).
claims.source: Interestingly, while paclitaxel-bound microtubules show a reduced microtubule radius of 10.97±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.21), docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a radius of 11.53±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.9), which is similar to the value obtained for GDP-microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claims.claim: Docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a radius of 11.53±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.9), which is similar to the value obtained for GDP-microtubules.
claims.source: Interestingly, while paclitaxel-bound microtubules show a reduced microtubule radius of 10.97±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.21), docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a radius of 11.53±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.9), which is similar to the value obtained for GDP-microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claims.claim: Lattice expansion by paclitaxel occurred either when the drug was added before the polymerization reaction was started with GTP- or GDP-tubulin, or when it was added to preformed microtubules.
claims.source: In the case of paclitaxel, this expansion occurred either when the drug was added before the polymerization reaction was started with GTP- or GDP-tubulin, or when it was added to preformed microtubules, in consonance with the rapid structural transitions of microtubules observed upon taxane addition (Díaz et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements and supported by a literature citation.

claims.claim: Microtubules with bound 2a, 2b, or baccatin III showed similar lattice expansion as those bound to paclitaxel or docetaxel.
claims.source: Interestingly, microtubules with bound 2a, 2b, or baccatin III showed similar lattice expansion as those bound to paclitaxel or docetaxel.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements shown in Figure 7 and Table 2.

claims.claim: The diffraction patterns of microtubules stabilized with 2a or 2b showed a diffuse 1 nm layer line that reflects variations in the tubulin monomer rise, in contrast to those bound by paclitaxel and docetaxel, which displayed a sharp band.
claims.source: Note that the diffraction patterns of microtubules stabilized with 2a or 2b showed a diffuse 1 nm layer line that reflects variations in the tubulin monomer (and consequently dimer) rise, in clear contrast to those bound by paclitaxel and docetaxel, which displayed a sharp band, that is, a robust monomer rise.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the X-ray fiber diffraction patterns.

claims.claim: Taxanes with or without a C13 side chain have the capacity to expand the microtubule lattice and thus affect longitudinal tubulin contacts along protofilaments.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that taxanes with or without a C13 side chain have the capacity to expand the microtubule lattice and thus affect longitudinal tubulin contacts along protofilaments.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the X-ray fiber diffraction results.

claims.claim: The nature of the C13 side chain can affect the radius of a microtubule and thus lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments.
claims.source: They further indicate that the nature of the C13 side chain can affect the radius of a microtubule and thus lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the X-ray fiber diffraction results showing different radii for paclitaxel vs. docetaxel-bound microtubules.

claims.claim: Microtubules assembled in the presence of baccatin III display the same radius as paclitaxel-bound microtubules.
claims.source: We note, however, that microtubules assembled in the presence of baccatin III, which lacks a C13 side chain, display the same radius as paclitaxel-bound microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claims.claim: The presence of a C13 side chain per se does not seem to modulate lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments.
claims.source: Thus, the presence of a C13 side chain per se does not seem to modulate lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that baccatin III (lacking C13 side chain) has the same radius as paclitaxel-bound microtubules.

claims.claim: The βM loop is the most flexible region in MD simulations of the tubulin dimer model.
claims.source: In our simulations of the tubulin dimer model, we found that the βM loop is the most flexible region (Figure 8 top), in good accord with the fact that no density is usually observed for this β-tubulin element in most crystallographic structures.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: During MD simulations, the βM loop was not structured as an α-helix in any of the models studied; instead, it assumed a relatively stable, extended hairpin conformation that interacted with and blocked access to the taxane site.
claims.source: During the course of the MD simulations, this loop was not structured as an α-helix in any of the models studied; instead, it was found to assume a relatively stable, extended hairpin conformation that interacted with and blocked access to the taxane site.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claims.claim: When the βM loop was initially modeled as an α-helix, this secondary structure element was rapidly lost during the simulated trajectory regardless of whether or not baccatin III, 2a, or paclitaxel was bound at the taxane site.
claims.source: Even when the βM loop was initially modeled as an α-helix (as present in all microtubule structures solved by cryoelectron microscopy; Alushin et al., 2014; Kellogg et al., 2017; Debs et al., 2020; Manka and Moores, 2018), this secondary structure element was rapidly lost during the simulated trajectory (Figure 8, bottom) regardless of whether or not baccatin III, 2a, or paclitaxel was bound at the taxane site (Figure 9AB).
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claims.claim: The bound taxanes do not establish any long-lasting hydrogen-bonding interactions with the amino acids making up the βM loop so as to stabilize it into an α-helix, as epothilone A and zampanolide do.
claims.source: One likely reason for this behavior is that the bound taxanes do not establish any long-lasting hydrogen-bonding interactions with the amino acids making up this loop (βL275-βL286) so as to stabilize it into an α-helix, as epothilone A and zampanolide do (Prota et al., 2013a).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results and supported by a literature citation.

claims.claim: The β-hairpin conformation of the βM loop may compete efficiently with the binding of ligands to the taxane site.
claims.source: Therefore, the β-hairpin conformation of the βM loop may compete efficiently with the binding of ligands to the taxane site (Animation 1Animation 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results shown in Animation 1.

claims.claim: The free energy of ligand binding to tubulin dimers with a βM loop partially occluding the taxane site would be expected to be much lower (in the 10³–10⁴ M⁻¹ range) than the free energy of binding to microtubules.
claims.source: As a consequence, the free energy of ligand binding to tubulin dimers with a βM loop partially occluding the taxane site would be expected to be much lower (in the 103–104 M–1 range) than the free energy of binding to microtubules, as is indeed the case (Díaz et al., 1993; Canales et al., 2014; Canales et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results and supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: Paclitaxel can adopt alternatively collapsed conformations in solution that are different from its bioactive, tubulin-bound T-shape conformation.
claims.source: When considering paclitaxel, entry into the taxane site is further hampered by the fact that this bulky and highly hydrophobic molecule can adopt alternatively collapsed conformations in solution that are different from its bioactive, tubulin-bound T-shape conformation (Snyder et al., 2001; Coderch et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: The alternative paclitaxel conformations that are inexistent in the case of baccatin III or 2a further reduce the apparent binding affinity below the solubility limit of the ligand.
claims.source: The alternative paclitaxel conformations that are inexistent in the case of baccatin III or 2a further reduce the apparent binding affinity below the solubility limit of the ligand (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: The less stringent requirements of the less bulky baccatin III and 2a molecules to bind compared to paclitaxel may explain the success in obtaining co-crystal structures with tubulin.
claims.source: Conversely, we think that the less stringent requirements of the less bulky baccatin III and 2a molecules to bind as compared to paclitaxel (Figure 10) may explain the success in obtaining co-crystal structures with tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and MD simulations.

claims.claim: The intermolecular hydrogen bond involving the oxetane O5 and the backbone NH of βT276 is a common feature to all three tubulin-taxane complexes.
claims.source: The intermolecular hydrogen bond involving the oxetane O5 and the backbone NH of βT276 is a common feature to all three tubulin-taxane complexes, both in crystals (baccatin III and 2a) and throughout the simulated MD trajectories (all three ligands).
claims.evidence: This is observed in both crystal structures and MD simulations.

claims.claim: Paclitaxel and 2a establish two other long-lived hydrogen bonds during MD simulations: O4':(NE2)βH229 and O2':(O=C)βR369.
claims.source: Paclitaxel and 2a establish two other long-lived hydrogen bonds during our simulations, namely O4':(NE2)βH229 and O2':(O=C)βR369, which may involve – depending on context – a βR369-βG370 backbone rearrangement.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claims.claim: The hydroxyl group at C13 of baccatin III alternates between acting as a direct or water-mediated hydrogen bond donor or an acceptor to/from (NE2)βH229 and (O=C)βR369, respectively.
claims.source: In turn, the hydroxyl group at C13 of baccatin III alternates between acting as a direct or water-mediated hydrogen bond donor or an acceptor to/from (NE2)βH229 and (O=C)βR369, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claims.claim: Paclitaxel binds better to straight tubulin and promotes tubulin assembly by lowering the critical concentration for tubulin assembly.
claims.source: It has been reported previously that paclitaxel binds better to straight tubulin and promote tubulin assembly (i.e., they lower the critical concentration for tubulin assembly Díaz et al., 1993; Buey et al., 2005) being therefore able to prevent the straight-to-curved conformational transition in GDP-bound microtubules (Elie-Caille et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: MD simulations indicate that protofilaments are curved both in the absence and in the presence of paclitaxel.
claims.source: However, our simulations indicate that protofilaments are curved both in the absence and in the presence of paclitaxel (Figure 9D), which suggests little or no direct influence of taxanes on the straight-to-curved conformational transition of tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: In MD simulations of the taxane-bound protofilament, the occupancy of the taxane site by the ligand constrains the available conformational space of the βM loop compared to that of the apo form, but the loop still fails to adopt a well-defined secondary structure in the absence of additional stabilizing interactions with a neighboring protofilament.
claims.source: On the other hand, and similar to unassembled tubulin, although in our simulations of the taxane-bound protofilament the occupancy of the taxane site by the ligand constrains the available conformational space of the βM loop compared to that of the apo form, the loop still fails to adopt a well-defined secondary structure in the absence of additional stabilizing interactions with a neighboring protofilament.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claims.claim: The solvent-exposed paclitaxel-bound βM loop is not permanently structured as an α-helix in MD simulations of the minimalist microtubule lattice model.
claims.source: We found that the solvent-exposed paclitaxel-bound βM loop is not permanently structured as an α-helix, as expected, and that the major ligand interactions at site 2 are essentially the same as in the paclitaxel-bound αβ-tubulin heterodimer and the protofilament model (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: In the interfacial taxane-binding site 1, dispersion forces, additional H-bonds, the hydrophobic effect, and decreased ligand entropy confer to the studied compounds higher binding free energies and longer residence times relative to the tubulin dimer and the exposed taxane site 2.
claims.source: On the other hand, in site 1 dispersion forces, additional H-bonds, the hydrophobic effect, and decreased ligand entropy confer to the studied compounds (paclitaxel, baccatin III, and 2a) higher binding free energies and longer residence times (i.e., lower koff values) relative to the tubulin dimer and the exposed taxane site 2 (Figure 11).
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results and binding energy calculations shown in Figure 11.

claims.claim: The three H-bond-mediated anchoring points O5:(NH)βT276, O4':(NE2)βH229, and O2':(O=C)βR369 are the same as those observed in the microtubule-paclitaxel complex structure.
claims.source: The three H-bond-mediated anchoring points, namely O5:(NH)βT276, O4':(NE2)βH229, and O2':(O=C)βR369, are the same as those observed in the microtubule-paclitaxel complex structure (Kellogg et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results and supported by a literature citation.

claims.claim: The hydrogen bond between the amide carbonyl O4' and the imidazole Nε of βHis229 is maintained in all the 2a and paclitaxel complexes studied even though this interaction fluctuates substantially.
claims.source: The hydrogen bond between the amide carbonyl O4' and the imidazole Nε of βHis229 is maintained in all the 2a and paclitaxel complexes studied even though this interaction fluctuates substantially, as does the stacking of βHis229 on the benzoyl phenyl ring.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claims.claim: The most important interaction that is strengthened laterally when a taxane is bound involves βTyr283, whose position in the βM loop is fixed by segment 85QIFR88 of loop βT3 from the neighboring β-tubulin subunit.
claims.source: However, the most important interaction that is strengthened laterally when a taxane is bound is that involving βTyr283, whose position in the βM loop is fixed by segment 85QIFR88 of loop βT3 from the neighboring β-tubulin subunit, as seen previously for other taxane-site ligands like, for example, zampanolide and taccalonolide AJ (Sánchez-Murcia et al., 2019; Figure 11).
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 11 and supported by a literature citation.

claims.claim: MD simulations consistently reproduce the axial lattice expansion observed upon paclitaxel binding.
claims.source: Importantly, our simulations consistently reproduce the axial lattice expansion observed upon paclitaxel binding (Arnal and Wade, 1995; Alushin et al., 2014; Estévez-Gallego et al., 2020; Kellogg et al., 2017; Debs et al., 2020; Manka and Moores, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results and supported by multiple literature citations.

claims.claim: The expansion mainly originates from displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop caused by the Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement in the βR369-βG370 stretch.
claims.source: We found that the expansion mainly originates from displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop caused by the Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement in the βR369-βG370 stretch.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claims.claim: The βS9-βS10 loop acts as a lid covering and stapling the bound taxanes in their final location.
claims.source: Because the βS9-βS10 loop acts as a lid covering and stapling the bound taxanes in their final location, this motion propagates toward the attached α-tubulin subunit so that the distance between the α1- and β2-tubulin subunits of two longitudinally aligned, consecutive tubulin dimers increases by roughly 2 Å as compared to the unbound filament (Figure 9E), a feature that could not be detected in the taxane-bound crystal structures of curved tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: The distance between the α1- and β2-tubulin subunits of two longitudinally aligned, consecutive tubulin dimers increases by roughly 2 Å upon taxane binding as compared to the unbound filament.
claims.source: Because the βS9-βS10 loop acts as a lid covering and stapling the bound taxanes in their final location, this motion propagates toward the attached α-tubulin subunit so that the distance between the α1- and β2-tubulin subunits of two longitudinally aligned, consecutive tubulin dimers increases by roughly 2 Å as compared to the unbound filament (Figure 9E), a feature that could not be detected in the taxane-bound crystal structures of curved tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: The baccatin III core of paclitaxel is responsible for filling most of the taxane site and for the key O5:NH(βT276) hydrogen-bonding interaction that is established between taxanes and β-tubulin.
claims.source: Our results reveal that the baccatin III core of paclitaxel is responsible for filling most of the taxane site and for the key O5:NH(βT276) hydrogen-bonding interaction that is established between taxanes and β-tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical results.

claims.claim: The O5:NH(βT276) hydrogen-bonding interaction has only a marginal effect on the drug's microtubule-stabilizing effect.
claims.source: However, this interaction has only a marginal effect on the drug's microtubule-stabilizing effect (Parness et al., 1982; Lataste et al., 1984; Kingston, 2000), which requires the C13 side chain to increase the selectivity of the drugs for microtubules over unassembled tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: The C13 side chain is required to increase the selectivity of taxanes for microtubules over unassembled tubulin.
claims.source: However, this interaction has only a marginal effect on the drug's microtubule-stabilizing effect (Parness et al., 1982; Lataste et al., 1984; Kingston, 2000), which requires the C13 side chain to increase the selectivity of the drugs for microtubules over unassembled tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical results.

claims.claim: Ring A of paclitaxel precludes binding of the drug to the T2R-TTL and TD1 crystals.
claims.source: On the other hand, we found that ring A of paclitaxel precludes binding of the drug to the T2R-TTL and TD1 crystals, while two taxanes with a modified, smaller C13 side chain (2a and 2b) can bind due to the reduced size of their 3'-acylamino substituents and increased flexibility relative to paclitaxel.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The smaller substituents of 2a and 2b allow the newly synthesized taxane derivatives to bind to curved, unassembled tubulin while keeping their binding poses very similar to that described for paclitaxel when bound to straight tubulin in microtubules.
claims.source: These smaller substituents allow the newly synthesized taxane derivatives to bind to curved, unassembled tubulin − while keeping their binding poses very similar to that described for paclitaxel when bound to straight tubulin in microtubules − by allowing adaptation of the whole ligand to a rearranged βR369-βG370 backbone in the crystal lattice.
claims.evidence: This is based on the structural results.

claims.claim: The selective recognition of microtubules by taxanes arises from the differential interaction of the bulky C13 side chains with straight and curved tubulin.
claims.source: Regarding the selective recognition of microtubules by taxanes, we found that it arises from two different terms. The first one is the differential interaction of the bulky C13 side chains with straight and curved tubulin.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural analyses.

claims.claim: Upon transition to the microtubule-assembled, straight tubulin state, the space around the C13 side chain is narrowed down by the side chains of βD26, βK19, βE22, and βH229 to form a favorable environment for the interaction with ring A, which may lock the paclitaxel-bound tubulin in the straight conformation.
claims.source: Upon transition to the microtubule-assembled, straight tubulin state, this space is narrowed down by the side chains of βD26, βK19, βE22, and βH229 to form a favorable environment for the interaction with ring A, which may lock the paclitaxel-bound tubulin in the straight conformation (Figure 12B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figure 12B.

claims.claim: In the absence of the C13 side chain or in the presence of less bulky moieties at the ring A position, ligand binding is likely to be less affected by the curved-to-straight conformational transition.
claims.source: In the absence of the C13 side chain (baccatin III) or in the presence of less bulky and more 'articulated' moieties at the ring A position (2a and 2b; their substituents at the N3 position have a rotatable bond in the middle), ligand binding is likely to be less affected by the curved-to-straight conformational transition, since much looser interactions can still be established with the charged residue side chains of the βS9-βS10 loop and helix H1 through water molecules (Figure 3B, Figure 12A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figures 3B and 12A.

claims.claim: Occupancy of the taxane site by the βM loop in the absence of lateral contacts is a general mechanism that accounts for the loss of at least four orders of magnitude in affinity when binding to unassembled tubulin relative to microtubules for all taxane-site ligands.
claims.source: A second term that accounts for selectivity is occupancy of the taxane site by the βM loop in the absence of lateral contacts, which would be a general mechanism that accounts for the loss of at least four orders of magnitude in affinity when binding to unassembled tubulin relative to microtubules for all taxane-site ligands, including paclitaxel, docetaxel (Díaz et al., 1993), discodermolide (Canales et al., 2011), epothilones (Canales et al., 2014), and 2a (this paper).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results and supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: In assembled microtubules the βM loop is structured as an α-helix and the preorganized taxane site is empty and ready to accommodate a ligand.
claims.source: Whereas in assembled microtubules the βM loop is structured as an α-helix and the preorganized taxane site is empty and ready to accommodate a ligand, in the unassembled tubulin dimer − as well as in the models of isolated protofilaments and the solvent-exposed site of the minimalist microtubule representation − this same loop displays a large conformational heterogeneity and can adopt a hairpin conformation that allows it to interact with the taxane site and thus to inhibit ligand binding (Figure 11).
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 11.

claims.claim: The conformational freedom of the βM loop in unassembled tubulin allows it to occupy the taxane-binding pocket in such a way as to preclude (or compete with) ligand binding.
claims.source: The MD analysis indicates that the conformational freedom of the βM loop in unassembled tubulin allows it to occupy the taxane-binding pocket in such a way as to preclude (or compete with) ligand binding.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results.

claims.claim: The free energy contribution of taxane-site ligands for microtubule assembly arises from the preferential recognition of the taxane-site conformation present in microtubules.
claims.source: On the other hand, the free energy contribution of taxane-site ligands for microtubule assembly arises from the preferential recognition of the taxane-site conformation present in microtubules (Nogales et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claims.claim: The βM loop is an essential structural element for the mode of action of paclitaxel and other clinically used taxanes.
claims.source: Our results point to the βM loop as an essential structural element for the mode of action of paclitaxel and other clinically used taxanes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined structural and computational results.

claims.claim: Baccatin III is able to reduce the flexibility of the βM loop by inducing a partial structuring of its N-terminal region.
claims.source: Our high-resolution structural analysis of baccatin III in complex with tubulin suggests that even this simplified taxane is able to reduce the flexibility of the βM loop by inducing a partial structuring of its N-terminal region.
claims.evidence: This is based on the crystal structure analysis.

claims.claim: Paclitaxel and the novel taxanes reported here affect interprotofilament contacts so as to promote microtubule stability through interactions with the N-terminal section of the βM loop.
claims.source: This observation suggests that paclitaxel and the novel taxanes reported here indeed affect interprotofilament contacts so as to promote microtubule stability through interactions with the N-terminal section of the βM loop, in good agreement with observations reported previously (Debs et al., 2020; Manka and Moores, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from X-ray fiber diffraction results and supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: Binding of taxanes to assembled microtubules results in a displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop, which promotes a lattice expansion.
claims.source: Finally, we found that binding of taxanes to assembled microtubules results in a displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop, which promotes a lattice expansion.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction data and MD simulations.

claims.claim: Lattice expansion is a general consequence of taxane binding and does not require the presence of a C13 side chain.
claims.source: Our present results reinforce the view that lattice expansion is indeed a general consequence of taxane binding and does not require the presence of a C13 side chain.
claims.evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction data showing expansion with baccatin III.

claims.claim: Lattice expansion is not an important factor contributing to the mechanism of microtubule stabilization by paclitaxel.
claims.source: Since baccatin III is essentially biologically inert (Parness et al., 1982; Lataste et al., 1984; Kingston, 2000; Andreu and Barasoain, 2001), our data further indicate that lattice expansion is not an important factor contributing to the mechanism of microtubule stabilization by paclitaxel.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that baccatin III causes lattice expansion but is biologically inactive.

claims.claim: In solution, it is the (O=C)βR369 that consistently acts as the hydrogen bond acceptor for the O2' hydroxyl of taxanes.
claims.source: Although in the complexes with 2a and 2b − but not in that with baccatin III − the crystal structures show that (NH)βG370 hydrogen bonds to the taxane side chain, the simulated complexes indicate that in solution it is the (O=C)βR369 that consistently acts as the hydrogen bond acceptor for the O2' hydroxyl of taxanes.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claims.claim: The βS9-βS10 loop is a major structural element that changes on taxane binding, and this change is transmitted to the following α-tubulin subunits on both sides, hence the stretching or longitudinal expansion of the concatenated tubulin dimers.
claims.source: In our view, these findings point to the βS9-βS10 loop as a major structural element that changes on taxane binding, and this change is transmitted to the following α-tubulin subunits on both sides, hence the stretching or longitudinal expansion of the concatenated tubulin dimers.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results.

claims.claim: The Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement in the βR369-βG370 stretch upon cooling down the tubulin-paclitaxel and baccatin III complex points to expansion of the cavity and consolidation of the hydrogen-bonding network as the main factors responsible for this conformational change.
claims.source: The fact that we observed the Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement in the βR369-βG370 stretch upon cooling down the tubulin-paclitaxel and baccatin III complex obtained after the TMD procedure (Animation 2 and Animation 3) points to expansion of the cavity and consolidation of the hydrogen-bonding network as the main factors responsible for this conformational change.
claims.evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Animations 2 and 3.

claims.claim: The core moiety of paclitaxel provides the main tubulin-interaction network while its C13 side chain enables selective recognition of the prestructured βM loop of the microtubule-assembled tubulin state.
claims.source: Our structural analyses further suggest a mode of action of paclitaxel by means of which its core moiety provides the main tubulin-interaction network while its C13 side chain enables selective recognition of the prestructured βM loop of the microtubule-assembled tubulin state.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined structural and computational results.

claims.claim: Differential recognition of the prestructured βM loop by the C13 side chain is expected to promote microtubule formation and stabilization.
claims.source: Such differential recognition is expected to promote microtubule formation and stabilization.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural and computational results.

claims.claim: The longitudinal expansion of the microtubule lattices is not related to the microtubule stabilization mechanism of taxanes.
claims.source: On the other hand, the longitudinal expansion of the microtubule lattices arises from the accommodation of the taxane core within the site, a process that is, however, not related to the microtubule stabilization mechanism of taxanes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that baccatin III causes expansion but is inactive.

results.result: High-resolution crystal structures of taxane-tubulin complexes were obtained: baccatin III at 1.9 Å (PDB ID 8BDE), compound 2a at 1.95 Å (PDB ID 8BDF), and compound 2b at 2.35 Å (PDB ID 8BDG).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C29, C37, and C38 report crystallographic structures with resolution data provided in Table 1 and electron density maps shown in Figure 2. The structures are deposited in the PDB with appropriate validation metrics (R-factors, completeness, etc.), supporting the successful determination of these complexes.

results.result: Baccatin III and compound 2a bind to unassembled tubulin with measurable affinities (Kb 3.0±0.5 × 10³ M⁻¹ and 0.8±0.3 × 10³ M⁻¹, respectively), with 2a showing increased affinity compared to other paclitaxel analogs that could not be measured.
results.evaluation: Claims C28 and C35 report direct experimental binding measurements using centrifugation assays with appropriate controls and internal standards. Claim C36 is supported by the comparison showing measurable binding for 2a but not for N-AB-PT, Chitax 40, or Chitax 68, though the inference about 'increased affinity' is relative to detection limits rather than direct comparison.

results.result: Baccatin III binds to the taxane site of curved tubulin with specific molecular interactions: the C2-benzoyloxy ring C stacks between βH229 and βL275, the carbonyl oxygen forms a hydrogen bond to βR278, the oxetane and C13 hydroxyl accept hydrogen bonds from βT276 and βH229, and the C4 acetate occupies a hydrophobic pocket.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 describe detailed structural features observed in the 1.9 Å crystal structure (Figures 3A and 4A). The high resolution and clear electron density (Figure 2D) support these specific molecular interactions, which are standard observations from crystallographic data at this resolution.

results.result: Compound 2a engages in similar core interactions as baccatin III but with a ~20° tilt toward βH6/βS7, positioning it closer to paclitaxel's binding pose in straight tubulin, and forms water-mediated hydrogen bonds through its terminal ester moiety.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by structural comparisons with RMSD calculations (C42: 0.794 Å vs baccatin III, 0.845 Å vs paclitaxel) and crystallographic observations shown in Figures 3B and 4B. The structural superpositions and hydrogen bonding patterns are clearly documented in the electron density maps.

results.result: Compounds 2a and 2b do not form covalent adducts with β-tubulin; the continuous electron density observed represents a strong hydrogen bond rather than a covalent bond.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 is strongly supported by anomalous diffraction data at the bromine peak wavelength showing clear anomalous peaks at the expected positions (Figure 2G), which would not occur if covalent bond formation had displaced the bromine. Claim C40 is supported by refinement results showing better fit for the non-covalent model.

results.result: Taxane binding to curved tubulin induces conformational changes in the βT5 loop (oriented in 'out' conformation), partial structuring of the N-terminal βM loop (up to βR278), and changes in the βS9-βS10 loop (more prominent with 2a than baccatin III).
results.evaluation: Claims C51, C52, C54, C57, and C59 are supported by RMSD analysis shown in Figure 5, comparing apo and ligand-bound structures. The observations are consistent with crystallographic data showing well-defined electron density for the βT5 loop and N-terminal βM loop, but disorder in the remaining βM loop portion. The differential effects on βS9-βS10 are attributed to the presence/absence of the C13 side chain.

results.result: Taxane binding causes subtle global conformational rearrangements in β-tubulin: baccatin III induces a relative twist between N-terminal and intermediate domains, while 2a causes these domains to move slightly apart.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 6 and Videos 1-4. The domain movements are subtle but reproducible when structures are superimposed on the central βH7 helix, providing evidence for ligand-specific conformational effects.

results.result: Paclitaxel binding to straight tubulin in microtubules induces conformational changes in βT5 and βM loops similar to curved tubulin, but additionally affects the βS2-βS2' loop and βH11-βH12 helix region, suggesting effects on lateral contacts not detectable in curved tubulin crystals.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by RMSD analysis comparing paclitaxel-bound (PDB 6WVR) and apo (PDB 6DPV) microtubules, shown in Figure 4C-D. The additional conformational changes in regions involved in lateral contacts (βS2-βS2' loop) provide structural evidence for effects specific to the microtubule context.

results.result: GMPCPP-microtubules show increased tubulin dimer rise (0.24 nm increase from 8.12±0.02 to 8.36±0.02 nm) and radius (from 11.42±0.1 to 11.63±0.1 nm) compared to GDP-microtubules, consistent with previous studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2 and Figure 7. The results are consistent with multiple literature citations (Vale et al., 1994; Alushin et al., 2014; Hyman et al., 1992; Yajima et al., 2012), providing validation for the experimental approach.

results.result: Paclitaxel and docetaxel induce similar lattice expansion (0.24 nm) as GMPCPP, but differ in microtubule radius: paclitaxel reduces radius to 10.97±0.1 nm while docetaxel maintains a radius similar to GDP-microtubules (11.53±0.1 nm). Compounds 2a, 2b, and baccatin III show similar expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by X-ray fiber diffraction data in Table 2 and Figure 7. The measurements show consistent lattice expansion across different taxanes but differential effects on radius, suggesting distinct mechanisms. The expansion occurs regardless of when paclitaxel is added (C73), supporting a robust structural effect.

results.result: Microtubules stabilized with 2a or 2b show diffuse 1 nm layer lines reflecting variations in tubulin monomer rise, contrasting with sharp bands observed for paclitaxel and docetaxel.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 is supported by direct observation in X-ray fiber diffraction patterns. The diffuse vs. sharp layer lines indicate differences in structural homogeneity, suggesting that the modified C13 side chains in 2a/2b result in less uniform lattice parameters compared to clinical taxanes.

results.result: Taxanes with or without C13 side chains can expand microtubule lattices (affecting longitudinal contacts), while the nature of the C13 side chain affects microtubule radius (lateral contacts). However, the presence of a C13 side chain per se does not modulate lateral contacts, as baccatin III (lacking C13) shows the same radius as paclitaxel.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by X-ray fiber diffraction data showing expansion with baccatin III (C78, C120) despite its biological inactivity. The differential radius effects between paclitaxel and docetaxel (C71-C72) support C77, while the similarity between baccatin III and paclitaxel radii (C78) supports C79. These observations distinguish longitudinal from lateral effects.

results.result: MD simulations show the βM loop is highly flexible in unassembled tubulin, adopting a stable hairpin conformation that occludes the taxane site rather than an α-helix. Taxanes do not establish long-lasting hydrogen bonds to stabilize the loop as an α-helix, resulting in 10³-10⁴ M⁻¹ binding affinity to dimers.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 are supported by MD simulation data shown in Figures 8-9 and Animation 1. The simulations consistently show loss of α-helical structure and adoption of a hairpin conformation across all three ligands (baccatin III, 2a, paclitaxel). The predicted affinity range (C85) matches experimental measurements (C28, C35) and literature values, providing validation.

results.result: Paclitaxel adopts alternative collapsed conformations in solution different from its bioactive T-shape, further reducing binding affinity below solubility limits. The less bulky baccatin III and 2a have less stringent binding requirements, explaining successful co-crystallization.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by MD simulations (Figure 9C) showing conformational heterogeneity for paclitaxel but not for baccatin III or 2a, and by literature citations (Snyder et al., 2001; Coderch et al., 2013). This provides a mechanistic explanation for the differential crystallization success and is consistent with the experimental observations.

results.result: MD simulations identify key hydrogen bonds common to all taxane-tubulin complexes: O5:(NH)βT276 for all three ligands, O4':(NE2)βH229 and O2':(O=C)βR369 for paclitaxel and 2a, and alternating interactions for the C13 hydroxyl of baccatin III.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are supported by MD simulation trajectories showing persistent hydrogen bonds. These computational predictions are validated by crystallographic observations (C31, C33, C43) and are consistent with the microtubule-paclitaxel structure (Kellogg et al., 2017), providing convergent evidence.

results.result: MD simulations indicate protofilaments remain curved in both absence and presence of paclitaxel, and the βM loop fails to adopt well-defined secondary structure in protofilaments without lateral contacts, suggesting little direct influence of taxanes on tubulin straightness.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by MD simulation results shown in Figure 9D. The persistent curvature in both apo and ligand-bound protofilaments challenges the hypothesis that taxanes directly induce straightening, though this computational result should be interpreted cautiously as MD simulations may not fully capture long-timescale conformational transitions.

results.result: In the minimalist microtubule model, the interfacial taxane-binding site 1 shows higher binding affinity than the solvent-exposed site 2, with key interactions involving βTyr283 stabilized by lateral contacts. The three H-bond anchoring points match those in microtubule-paclitaxel structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are supported by MD simulations of the two-protofilament model shown in Figures 10-11. The differential binding energies between sites 1 and 2 (C96) and the identification of βTyr283 as a key residue (C99) are supported by per-residue energy decomposition. The consistency with cryo-EM structures (C97) provides validation.

results.result: MD simulations reproduce the observed axial lattice expansion upon paclitaxel binding, originating from displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop via Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement at βR369-βG370. This increases the distance between consecutive tubulin dimers by ~2 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are supported by MD simulations shown in Figure 9E that reproduce experimental X-ray fiber diffraction observations (C67, C70). The mechanistic explanation involving the βS9-βS10 loop and specific backbone rearrangement provides molecular detail not accessible from diffraction data alone, with the ~2 Å expansion matching experimental measurements.

results.result: Taxanes bind preferentially to microtubules over unassembled tubulin due to: (1) βM loop conformational reorganization that otherwise occludes the taxane site, and (2) bulky C13 side chains selectively recognizing the assembled state through interactions with βD26, βK19, βE22, and βH229 that form a favorable environment in straight tubulin.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C26, C109-C112 represent the major mechanistic conclusions supported by convergent evidence from crystallography (showing partial βM loop structuring), MD simulations (showing βM loop occlusion in dimers), binding measurements (showing 10³-10⁴ M⁻¹ for dimers vs higher for microtubules), and structural comparisons (Figures 3B, 12A-B). The two-term explanation is well-supported by the data.

results.result: The occupancy of the taxane site has no influence on the straightness of tubulin protofilaments, as MD simulations show curved protofilaments in both presence and absence of taxanes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C27, and C93 are based primarily on MD simulations (Figure 9D) showing persistent curvature. While the simulations are internally consistent, this conclusion contradicts some literature suggesting taxanes facilitate the curved-to-straight transition (C24, C92). The MD timescales (0.6-1.2 μs) may be insufficient to observe rare conformational transitions, and force field limitations could affect curvature predictions. Additional experimental validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Longitudinal expansion of microtubule lattices arises from accommodation of the taxane core (observed with baccatin III), but this expansion is not related to microtubule stabilization since baccatin III is biochemically inactive.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C119-C121, C127 are supported by X-ray fiber diffraction showing expansion with baccatin III (Table 2, Figure 7) despite its lack of biological activity (C8, supported by literature). This dissociation between lattice expansion and stabilization is a key finding. However, the mechanism by which expansion occurs (βS9-βS10 loop displacement, C101-C103) is based on MD simulations and could benefit from additional experimental validation.

results.result: The baccatin III core provides the main tubulin-interaction network and fills most of the taxane site, while the C13 side chain is required for selective recognition of the microtubule-assembled state and microtubule stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50, C104, C106, C125 synthesize structural and functional data showing that baccatin III binds with measurable affinity (C28) and induces similar core interactions (C41) but lacks stabilization activity (C8, C105). The C13 side chain's role in selectivity is supported by structural comparisons (C46-C47, C109-C111) and binding data (C35-C36). This structure-function relationship is well-supported.

results.result: Ring A of paclitaxel precludes binding to T2R-TTL and TD1 crystals, while compounds 2a and 2b with smaller, more flexible C13 substituents can bind to curved tubulin by allowing backbone rearrangement at βR369-βG370.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by the experimental observation that paclitaxel, docetaxel, and other taxanes with bulky C13 groups failed to yield crystal structures, while 2a and 2b succeeded. The structural explanation involving βR369-βG370 backbone adaptation is supported by crystallographic data (C37-C38) and MD simulations, though the inference about why paclitaxel fails is indirect.

results.result: The βM loop is an essential structural element for taxane action. Even baccatin III reduces βM loop flexibility by inducing partial N-terminal structuring, and taxanes affect interprotofilament contacts through interactions with the N-terminal βM loop section.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 are supported by crystallographic data showing partial βM loop structuring (C54), X-ray fiber diffraction showing effects on lateral contacts (C74-C75), and MD simulations showing βM loop dynamics (C80-C84). The conclusion is consistent with recent literature (Debs et al., 2020; Manka and Moores, 2018) cited in C118.

results.result: In solution, (O=C)βR369 acts as the hydrogen bond acceptor for taxane O2' hydroxyl (not (NH)βG370 as in crystals), and the βS9-βS10 loop is a major structural element transmitting conformational changes to adjacent α-tubulin subunits upon taxane binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 are supported by MD simulations showing consistent (O=C)βR369 hydrogen bonding despite crystallographic structures showing (NH)βG370 interactions. The Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement observed in TMD simulations (Animations 2-3) provides mechanistic insight into the expansion process. The discrepancy between crystal and solution structures is reasonable given crystal packing constraints.

results.result: In curved tubulin, the 3'-N-benzamido phenyl ring A of paclitaxel cannot establish favorable hydrogen bonds due to distance from helix H1. In straight tubulin, helix H1 moves closer to H7, forming a hydrophobic cavity that stabilizes ring A, with βD26 providing additional polar interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by structural comparisons between curved tubulin-2a (PDB 8BDF) and straight tubulin-paclitaxel (PDB 6WVR) structures shown in Figures 3B, 4B, and 12. The helix H1 movement and formation of the hydrophobic cavity provide a structural explanation for the preferential binding to straight tubulin, though the inference is based on static structures rather than dynamic measurements.

results.result: There is allosteric crosstalk between the taxane site and the βT5 loop, possibly via central helix βH7 and the guanosine nucleotide bound to β-tubulin.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is inferred from the observation that the βT5 loop adopts an 'out' conformation in taxane-bound structures (C52) despite no direct contacts with the ligand. While the proposed pathway via βH7 and the nucleotide is plausible given the structural architecture, no direct evidence (e.g., mutagenesis, nucleotide exchange experiments) is provided to validate this allosteric mechanism. The claim remains speculative.

results.result: Background information on taxanes: paclitaxel is a microtubule-stabilizing chemotherapeutic drug on the WHO Essential Medicines list, used for treating solid tumors, though it causes peripheral neuropathy. Three taxanes are in clinical use: paclitaxel, docetaxel, and cabazitaxel.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C14 provide established background information supported by appropriate literature citations and general knowledge in the field. These claims set the context for the study but do not represent novel findings.

results.result: Literature review of prior structural and mechanistic studies: cryo-EM structures of taxane-microtubule complexes at 3-10 Å resolution suggest conflicting mechanisms (longitudinal vs. lateral effects), X-ray structures of non-taxane agents at 1.8-2.4 Å show different βM loop conformations, and tubulin displays curved vs. straight conformations related to assembly state.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C25 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims establish the knowledge gaps (C2, C25) that motivate the current study, particularly the lack of high-resolution taxane-tubulin structures and conflicting mechanistic models.

results.result: Baccatin III is biochemically inactive and the O5:NH(βT276) hydrogen bond has only marginal effect on microtubule stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C105 are supported by multiple literature citations (Parness et al., 1982; Lataste et al., 1984; Kingston, 2000; Andreu and Barasoain, 2001). This established knowledge is critical for interpreting the significance of the baccatin III structure and the dissociation between binding and biological activity.

results.result: The absence of the C10 acetate in 2a relative to baccatin III has little impact on the conformation of secondary structural elements shaping the taxane site.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3C. The RMSD analysis and visual inspection show minimal conformational differences in the binding site architecture despite the chemical difference, validating the design strategy for 2a.

results.result: Partial βM loop structuring has been observed previously with dictyostatin and discodermolide, and taxane effects on the βM loop are consistent with paclitaxel stabilizing this element in two discrete conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by appropriate literature citations (Trigili et al., 2016; Prota et al., 2017; Debs et al., 2020) that provide context for the current observations. These claims connect the present findings to prior structural studies of taxane-site ligands.

results.result: The presence of a C13 side chain in 2a requires more room for accommodation inside the taxane site compared to baccatin III, explaining more prominent βS9-βS10 loop changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is a straightforward inference from the structural observations (C57) and the chemical structures of the ligands. The larger size of 2a compared to baccatin III provides a simple explanation for the differential conformational changes observed in the βS9-βS10 loop.

results.result: Literature reports that paclitaxel binds better to straight tubulin, promotes assembly by lowering critical concentration, and prevents straight-to-curved transitions. The free energy contribution for assembly arises from preferential recognition of the microtubule-assembled conformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92 and C115 accurately cite prior literature (Díaz et al., 1993; Buey et al., 2005; Elie-Caille et al., 2007; Nogales et al., 1999) establishing the preferential binding to assembled tubulin. These claims provide context for interpreting the current structural and computational findings.

results.result: Differential recognition of the prestructured βM loop by the C13 side chain is expected to promote microtubule formation and stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claim C126 is a reasonable inference from the combined structural and computational results (C4-C5, C26, C109-C112, C125) showing that the C13 side chain enables selective recognition of the assembled state. While the expectation is logical, direct experimental validation of this mechanism (e.g., through mutagenesis or kinetic studies) would strengthen the conclusion.
